routines.name: Stance and Balance Basics
routines.summary: Develop a stable, balanced stance to help improve cue delivery, accuracy and consistency on every shot.
routines.description:
Your stance is the foundation of your snooker technique. A stable and comfortable position allows your cue to travel smoothly along the shot line, helping you deliver the cue straight and consistently.

If your balance shifts or your head moves during the shot, your cue delivery can be affected, leading to inaccurate contact and inconsistent results.

There is no single perfect stance for everyone. Your height, build and flexibility will influence your positioning. The aim is to develop a stance that feels natural, keeps you balanced and can be repeated comfortably under pressure
routines.setup_instructions:
Use a selection of straightforward pots, including straight shots and slight angles. This allows you to concentrate on your body position rather than worrying about difficult potting challenges.

Whether you play right-handed or left-handed, the same principles apply. Your stance should be adapted to your dominant hand and natural comfort.
steps:
Position your feet:
- Right-handed players: Your left foot should be forward and slightly bent, while your right foot sits further back and remains relatively straight.

- Left-handed players: Your right foot should be forward and slightly bent, while your left foot sits further back and remains relatively straight.

Keep your feet comfortably apart and avoid locking your knees. Your stance should feel natural, stable and balanced rather than forced.
Find your balance: Keep your feet comfortably apart and distribute your weight evenly. Avoid stretching too far or feeling as though you might lose your balance during the shot.

Align your body: Choose your shot line while standing. As you lower into position, allow your body to settle naturally around that line without making unnecessary adjustments to your feet, hips or shoulders.
Set your bridge hand: Place your non-cueing hand firmly on the table to create a stable bridge. Right-handed players use their left hand, while left-handed players use their right.
Keep your head still: Once down on the shot, keep your head and upper body as steady as possible throughout the cue action.
Hold your finish: After striking the cue ball, remain in position briefly. This helps you recognise whether your balance shifted or your body moved during delivery.
routines.success_criteria:
Complete 20–30 straightforward shots, concentrating on your stance rather than the outcome of the pot.

After each shot, ask yourself:
- Did I feel balanced and comfortable?
- Was my head still throughout the delivery?
- Did I maintain my position after striking the cue ball?
- Did I feel any unnecessary tension?

Count the number of shots where you successfully maintain a stable, balanced stance and hold your position through the delivery.

routines.name: Grip Fundamentals
routines.summary: Develop a relaxed, controlled grip that allows the cue to move freely and deliver a smooth, consistent strike.
routines.description:
Your grip plays an important role in the accuracy, timing and consistency of your cue action. Holding the cue too tightly can create tension in your wrist and forearm, restricting movement and making it harder to deliver the cue smoothly.

On the other hand, holding the cue too loosely can make it difficult to maintain control, particularly during longer or more powerful shots.

The aim is to find a comfortable, secure grip that allows your cueing arm to move naturally. Your grip should remain relaxed during feathering and throughout delivery, without unnecessarily tightening or changing pressure at the point of impact.
routines.setup_instructions:
Choose a straightforward pot that you can repeat comfortably, ideally a straight pot at short or medium distance.

Use the same shot throughout the exercise so you can concentrate on your grip rather than adjusting your aim or shot selection.

The principles apply to both right-handed and left-handed players. Simply mirror the positioning of your cueing hand.
steps: Find your natural grip: Hold the cue in your dominant hand, positioning it comfortably around the butt of the cue. Your fingers should wrap naturally around it without squeezing tightly.
Keep your grip relaxed: Avoid clenching your hand or creating unnecessary tension in your wrist and forearm. You should feel in control of the cue without restricting its movement.
Relax during feathering: Practise your feathering action while keeping your grip consistent and relaxed. Your wrist and forearm should be able to move freely.
Deliver smoothly: As you begin your final delivery, allow your cueing arm to accelerate naturally. Avoid tightening your grip suddenly or forcing the cue through the shot.
Maintain control: Keep your grip secure throughout the strike and follow-through. The cue should feel stable in your hand without being squeezed.
Experiment with pressure: Try a few shots using slightly different grip pressures. Notice whether a tighter or looser hold affects your cue delivery, accuracy or comfort.
routines.success_criteria:
Complete 20–30 shots using the same repeatable pot.

Focus on:
- Keeping your grip relaxed during feathering.
- Maintaining a consistent grip throughout delivery.
- Avoiding unnecessary wrist and forearm tension.
- Producing a smooth, straight cue action.

Finishing each shot without feeling that you have forced the cue.

Count the number of shots where you maintain a relaxed, controlled grip and deliver the cue smoothly.

The aim is to develop a repeatable grip that feels natural rather than chasing a particular grip pressure.

routines.name: Bridge Fundamentals
routines.summary: Learn how to build a stable bridge that supports and guides your cue, improving accuracy, control and consistency.
routines.description:
Your bridge hand provides the support and guidance your cue needs to travel smoothly towards the cue ball. A stable bridge helps maintain a consistent cueing line, while an unstable or poorly positioned bridge can cause the cue to move off line during delivery.

There are several bridge styles used in snooker, each suited to different shots and situations. This guide introduces the main techniques, including the open bridge, closed bridge, cushion bridge and raised bridge.

The aim is to understand how to construct each bridge, when to use it and how to keep your hand stable throughout the shot.
routines.setup_instructions:
Choose a straightforward pot that allows you to practise your bridge without worrying about difficult positioning.

You will also need a ball close to a cushion and an object ball positioned to practise a raised bridge over it.

Practise each bridge type using a comfortable shot, focusing on stability and a clear path for the cue.
steps: Open Bridge: Place your non-cueing hand flat on the table with your fingers spread comfortably. Raise your thumb against the side of your index finger to create a groove for the cue to rest in. Keep your palm and fingers firmly supported by the table.

Closed Bridge: Start with your hand planted on the table. Curl your index finger over the cue and bring it towards your thumb to form a closed loop around the cue. This provides additional guidance and helps keep the cue aligned during delivery.

Cushion Bridge: When the cue ball is close to a cushion, place your hand on top of the cushion and use your fingers and thumb to create a stable support for the cue. Adjust your hand position to maintain a comfortable and level cueing line.

Raised Bridge: When another ball obstructs your normal cueing path, raise your bridge hand and support the cue using your thumb and fingers. Keep the cue stable and avoid allowing it to wobble during delivery.

Adjusting Bridge Height: Experiment with slightly different bridge heights when practising stun, screw and topspin shots. Keep your bridge firm and stable while allowing enough clearance for the cue to move freely.
Maintain Stability: Regardless of which bridge you use, keep your bridge hand planted and avoid lifting or shifting it during the final delivery and follow-through.
routines.success_criteria:
Complete 20–30 shots, dividing your practice between the different bridge types.

Try to include:
- 5 shots using an open bridge.
- 5 shots using a closed bridge.
- 5 shots using a cushion bridge.
- 5 shots using a raised bridge.

Additional shots using whichever bridge type you find most difficult.

Focus on keeping your bridge hand stable, maintaining a consistent cueing line and delivering the cue smoothly.

Count the number of shots where your bridge remains stable throughout delivery and provides a clear, controlled cueing path.

routines.name: Alignment and Sighting Basics
routines.summary: Develop a consistent aiming routine by learning to identify the shot line, visualise the contact point and align your body and cue correctly.
routines.description:
Accurate potting starts before you even get down on the shot. Good sighting helps you identify the correct contact point on the object ball, while proper alignment ensures your cue is positioned along your intended shot line.

Rushing this process or making adjustments once you are down can lead to steering, inconsistent cue delivery and missed pots.

Every player has slightly different visual preferences, including dominant-eye positioning and how they approach the shot. The aim is to develop a repeatable routine that feels natural and allows you to see and deliver the shot with confidence.
routines.setup_instructions:
Use a selection of straightforward pots at different angles and distances. Include straight pots, half-ball cuts and three-quarter-ball cuts to practise identifying different contact points.

Keep the shots manageable so you can concentrate on your sighting and alignment rather than difficult potting challenges.
steps: Identify the shot line: Stand behind the cue ball and object ball, looking towards the intended pocket. Visualise the path the object ball needs to take to reach the pocket.
Find the contact point: Identify where the cue ball needs to strike the object ball to produce the intended pot. Consider whether the shot requires a full-ball, half-ball or thinner contact.
Visualise the aim: Take a moment to picture the intended contact point and the path of the object ball. Make your aiming decision before lowering into your stance.
Approach the shot: Step into your stance along the intended shot line. Position your body and cue naturally without making unnecessary adjustments once you are down.
Check your alignment: Ensure your cue is travelling along your intended delivery line. Your head and eyes should be positioned comfortably so you can see the shot clearly.
Develop a consistent visual routine: Use your final practice strokes to confirm your aim and build confidence. Avoid repeatedly changing your intended contact point during the final delivery.
Review your results: If you miss, consider whether you struck the object ball too thick, too thin or with the wrong pace. Use this feedback to improve your next attempt.
routines.success_criteria:
Complete 20–30 shots using a mixture of straight, half-ball and three-quarter-ball pots.

Before each shot:
-Identify the intended pocket.
-Visualise the object-ball path.
-Decide on the contact point.
-Set your stance and alignment.
-Commit to your chosen line before delivering the cue.

After each attempt, assess whether your miss was caused by aiming, alignment, cue delivery or pace.

Count the number of successful pots out of your total attempts.

Also pay attention to whether you correctly identified the intended contact point before getting down on the shot

routines.name: Cueing Action and Potting Basics
routines.summary: Develop a smooth, controlled and repeatable cue action to improve striking accuracy, potting consistency and confidence at the table.
routines.description:
Your cueing action is one of the most important parts of playing consistent snooker. Even with good alignment and a stable stance, poor cue delivery can cause the cue ball to travel off line, resulting in inaccurate contact and missed pots.

Common mistakes include rushing the final delivery, gripping the cue too tightly, decelerating before impact or moving the head and body during the shot.

This guide introduces the key stages of a reliable cue action, from feathering and timing to smooth acceleration and follow-through. The aim is to develop a natural rhythm that you can repeat on every shot, regardless of distance or difficulty.
routines.setup_instructions:
Begin with a selection of straightforward straight pots using centre-ball striking. Choose a comfortable distance and use the same shot repeatedly so you can concentrate on your cue action.

Once your delivery becomes consistent, introduce gentle stun and screw shots to understand how your cue action affects the cue ball.
steps: Settle into position: Establish your stance, grip, bridge and alignment before beginning your cue action. Make sure you feel balanced and comfortable.
Begin feathering: Move the cue smoothly backwards and forwards through your bridge. Keep your wrist and forearm relaxed, maintaining a consistent path along the intended shot line.
Develop your rhythm: Use your feathering strokes to become comfortable with the shot. Avoid rushing or making unnecessary movements.
Introduce a pause: Before your final delivery, pause briefly at the end of your backswing. This helps separate your preparation from the actual strike and gives you time to commit to the shot.
Deliver smoothly: Move the cue forward with controlled acceleration, striking the cue ball cleanly. Avoid jabbing at the ball or deliberately slowing down just before impact.
Follow through: Allow the cue to continue naturally along the shot line after contact. Avoid pulling the cue back immediately or cutting the follow-through short.
Hold your finish: Remain still for a moment after striking the cue ball. Check that your head stayed steady and your cue finished along the intended line.
Build consistency: Repeat the same routine across different shots. Once your plain-ball delivery is reliable, introduce stun, screw and topspin while maintaining the same fundamental cue action.
routines.success_criteria:
How to Practise

Complete 20–30 shots, beginning with straightforward centre-ball pots.

Focus on:
- Maintaining a consistent feathering rhythm.
- Pausing briefly before your final delivery.
- Keeping your cue on the intended shot line.
- Accelerating smoothly through the cue ball.
- Following through naturally.
- Keeping your head and body still until the shot is complete.

Once comfortable, introduce a few stun and screw shots without changing your fundamental delivery.

Count the number of shots where you successfully maintain a smooth, controlled and repeatable cue action.

routines.name: Head Position Fundamentals
routines.summary: Develop a consistent and comfortable head position to improve sighting, visual alignment and confidence when addressing the cue ball.
routines.description:
Your head position plays an important role in how you see and deliver each shot. If your head moves or changes position between shots, your visual perspective can change, making it harder to judge angles and maintain consistent alignment.

A stable head position helps keep your eyes, cue and intended shot line connected throughout the cue action.

There is no single head position that suits every player. Your height, build, neck flexibility and dominant eye can all influence where your head naturally sits. The aim is to find a comfortable position that provides a clear view of the shot without creating unnecessary tension.
routines.setup_instructions:
Use a selection of straightforward straight and slight-angle pots. Keep the cue-ball and object-ball positions simple so you can concentrate on your head position rather than the difficulty of the shot.

Practise from the same position initially, allowing you to develop a consistent head placement before introducing different angles.
steps: Establish your stance: Set your feet, bridge hand and body position before lowering into the shot. Make sure you are balanced and aligned with your intended shot line.
Lower your head naturally: Once your body is in position, bring your head down towards the cue. Avoid dropping your head too early or making unnecessary adjustments once you are settled.

Find your comfortable height: Position your head so you can see the cue ball and object ball clearly. Your chin may sit close to or lightly touch the cue, but avoid forcing it down or creating tension in your neck.

Check your eye line: Keep your eyes comfortably level and focused along the intended shot line. Your dominant eye may influence where your head naturally sits, so find a position that gives you a clear and consistent view.
Keep your head still: Once you are settled, avoid moving your head from side to side or lifting it during your feathering and final delivery.

Hold your position: After striking the cue ball, remain down on the shot until the object ball has reached its intended destination. This helps prevent premature head movement and encourages a more controlled delivery.
Build consistency: Repeat the same process across different shots. Your head position should feel familiar and comfortable each time you approach the table.
routines.success_criteria:
Count the number of shots where you maintain a stable and comfortable head position throughout your setup, delivery and follow-through.

A successful attempt should demonstrate:
- Consistent head height and positioning.
- A clear view of the intended shot line.
- Minimal movement during delivery.

A controlled finish without lifting your head prematurely.

routines.name: Straight Cueing Fundamentals
routines.summary: Develop a straight and consistent cue action to improve accuracy, striking quality and control over the cue ball.
routines.description:
Straight cueing is one of the foundations of good snooker technique. Your cue should travel smoothly along the intended shot line, allowing you to strike the cue ball accurately and consistently.

If your cue moves sideways during delivery, it can cause unwanted contact, inaccurate striking and inconsistent results. This becomes particularly noticeable when attempting to apply side spin or play more demanding positional shots.

Common issues include steering the cue, moving the elbow or wrist unnecessarily, and allowing the cue to move away from the intended line during the final delivery.

This guide teaches you how to recognise and correct these habits, developing a cue action that remains controlled from the backswing through to the follow-through.
routines.setup_instructions:
Begin with short, straight pots using centre-ball striking. Position the cue ball and object ball directly in line with a pocket, allowing you to concentrate on your cue movement.

Start at a comfortable distance and gradually increase the distance once you feel confident that your cue is travelling consistently.
steps: Establish your shot line: Stand behind the shot and identify the intended line between the cue ball, object ball and pocket. Set up naturally along this line.
Use centre-ball striking: Begin by aiming to strike the centre of the cue ball. This removes unnecessary spin variables and allows you to focus on the straightness of your delivery.
Check your bridge: Make sure your bridge provides a stable channel for the cue. The cue should be able to move backwards and forwards without excessive sideways movement.
Use slow-motion video from rear line to confirm whether cue tracks straight through strike.
Practise your feathering: Move the cue smoothly through your bridge, checking that it follows the same path during each practice stroke.
Deliver in a straight line: Move the cue forward smoothly towards the cue ball. Avoid steering, twisting your wrist or making unnecessary sideways adjustments during delivery.
Follow through naturally: Allow the cue to continue along the intended shot line after impact. Keep your head and body still while completing the movement.

Review your delivery: Pay attention to repeated miss patterns and consider whether your cue is moving off line. If possible, record your action from directly behind the shot line to review your cue movement.
Increase the distance: Once your cue action feels consistent on shorter pots, gradually increase the distance while maintaining the same delivery technique.
routines.success_criteria:
Complete 20–30 straight pots, beginning at a comfortable distance.

Focus on:
- Keeping the cue centred within your bridge
- Maintaining a consistent path during feathering.
- Avoiding sideways movement during the final delivery.
- Striking the centre of the cue ball.
- Following through along the intended shot line.
- Gradually increase the distance as your cueing becomes more consistent.

If possible, record a few shots from behind the cue to identify any repeated sideways movement.

Count the number of shots where you demonstrate a controlled, straight cue delivery and successfully pot the object ball.

Pay attention to whether your cue remains centred through the bridge and follows the intended shot line.

altVideo.title: Snooker Straight Cueing How To Practice

routines.name: Cue Ball Control Fundamentals
routines.summary: Learn how different striking points affect cue-ball movement, developing the foundations of positional play and spin control.
routines.description:
Cue-ball control is one of the most important skills in snooker. Potting a ball is only part of the shot; understanding where the cue ball will finish is what allows you to build breaks and control the table.

The position of your cue tip when striking the cue ball influences how it reacts after contact with an object ball. By learning to control plain-ball, follow, stun and screw shots, you can begin to predict and manage the cue ball's movement more effectively.

This guide introduces these fundamental techniques through simple, repeatable shots before progressing towards more advanced positional play.
routines.setup_instructions:
Choose a straightforward pot with the cue ball and object ball positioned in a comfortable, repeatable line towards a pocket.

Keep the object-ball position and shot distance consistent throughout the exercise. This allows you to focus on how different tip positions affect the cue ball after contact.
steps: Plain-Ball Contact: Begin by striking the centre of the cue ball. Observe how it travels after contacting the object ball. With a suitable delivery distance and speed, the cue ball will lose its forward and backward rotation and come to a natural stop near the point of contact.
Topspin (Follow): Strike slightly above the centre of the cue ball. This creates forward rotation, causing the cue ball to continue travelling forward after contacting the object ball.

Stun: Strike below centre with enough pace to maintain backspin until the cue ball reaches the object ball. The cue ball should stop close to the point of contact rather than running forward or drawing backwards.
Screw (Backspin): Strike below centre with a controlled delivery to create backspin. When the cue ball reaches the object ball with backspin remaining, it will travel backwards after contact.
Experiment with Pace: Repeat each shot using slightly different delivery speeds. Notice how distance, cue speed and tip position work together to change the cue ball's reaction.
Develop Prediction: Before each shot, decide where you expect the cue ball to finish. Compare your prediction with the actual result and adjust your understanding accordingly.
routines.success_criteria:
Complete 20–30 shots, dividing your practice between the four fundamental cue-ball reactions:

- Plain Ball – Strike the centre of the cue ball.
- Topspin – Strike above centre.
- Stun – Strike below centre with the correct pace to remove the cue ball's forward movement at impact.
- Screw – Strike below centre with sufficient backspin to draw the cue ball backwards after contact.

Keep the object-ball position consistent and experiment with different tip positions and delivery speeds.

Before every shot, predict where the cue ball will finish. This helps develop your understanding of cue-ball reactions rather than simply relying on trial and error.

Count the number of shots where you successfully produce the intended cue-ball reaction.

routines.name: Pre-Shot Routine Fundamentals
routines.summary: Develop a repeatable pre-shot routine so your decision, setup and delivery follow a consistent sequence.
routines.description:
A pre-shot routine connects your tactical decision with your technical execution. Having a consistent process helps prevent rushing difficult shots, overthinking straightforward ones and making unnecessary changes once you're down on the shot.

This guide introduces a simple routine that you can use in both practice and match play, helping you approach each shot with greater clarity and confidence.
routines.setup_instructions: Start with easy-to-medium pots so you can focus on the routine rather than shot difficulty. Use a variety of shots throughout the exercise, keeping the same sequence each time.
steps: Assess the shot: Stand behind the shot and decide what you want to achieve. Identify the contact point, intended potting line and desired cue-ball position.
Walk into the shot: Approach along your chosen shot line. Position your feet comfortably and establish your balance before lowering into your stance.
Settle and prepare: Build your bridge, bring the cue onto the intended line and use a few purposeful feathers to confirm your aim and feel comfortable.
Commit and deliver: Once settled, pause naturally and play the shot. Avoid changing your decision or making last-second adjustments unless something genuinely feels wrong.
Review: Hold your finish, observe the result and briefly consider whether you followed your routine. Then step away and begin again.
routines.success_criteria:
Play 15–20 straightforward pots, using your full pre-shot routine before every attempt. Vary the angle and distance slightly, but keep the sequence consistent.

Focus on making each step deliberate rather than rushing to get down on the shot. If you notice yourself skipping a step or changing your aim at the last moment, reset and concentrate on the process for your next attempt.

Count each shot where you complete the full routine in the correct order and deliver without unnecessary hesitation or last-second changes.

The pot does not have to be successful. The focus is on building a consistent process, not measuring potting accuracy.

routines.name: The Snooker Line Up
routines.summary: Classic 15-red line-up to build break rhythm and positional discipline.
routines.description: Use a full line of reds through the middle of the table to train break-building patterns with all colours on their spots.
routines.setup_instructions: Place all colours on their spots. Set 15 reds in a straight central line: 2 behind the black (between the black spot and the top cushion), 4 between the black and pink, 7 between the pink and blue, and 2 between the blue and brown. Start from a chosen red, often the second red down from the black.
steps: Choose a consistent starting red and use it each visit so your scoring is comparable.
Pot red then colour while keeping the cue-ball in the open and away from cushions where possible.
If the break ends, reset the line-up and record the break or the number of reds cleared.
routines.success_criteria: Log your best visit out of 147, then track your average break across 5 visits.

routines.name: The Snooker T Line Up
routines.summary: Advanced T-shape break-building routine for close-control cue-ball work.
routines.description: The T Line-Up tests break-building around the pink area, with little room for error in angle and pace.
routines.setup_instructions: Place all colours on their spots. Set 15 reds in a T shape: reds spread left and right from the pink line, with a central stem running down towards the black.
steps: Start from a chosen red with the cue-ball in open space near the T formation.
Alternate red and colour while keeping the cue-ball under tight control around the T.
If you miss, reset and track either break score or reds remaining for comparison.
routines.success_criteria: Log your best visit out of 147, then note completed T clearances and controlled visits in 30 minutes.

routines.name: Mastering The Colours
routines.summary: Colour-clearance routine for cue-ball touch and end-of-frame planning.
routines.description: Clear the colours in order while keeping the cue-ball under close control from ball to ball.
routines.setup_instructions: Place all colours on their spots and start with the cue-ball in hand in the D.
steps: Call the intended cue-ball path before each colour.
Use controlled pace so recovery shots stay simple.
Restart the clearance after any miss or poor position.
routines.success_criteria: Number of full colour clearances completed in 20 minutes.

altVideo.title: Don't Make These Mistakes When Clearing the Colours

routines.name: 3 Reds + Colours Clearance
routines.summary: Short-format break-building with emphasis on colour choice and cue-ball placement.
routines.description: A compact break-building routine that creates realistic decisions over only a few reds.
routines.setup_instructions: Place 3 open reds around the pink and black area and keep all colours on their spots.
steps: Pot a red and choose the best available colour for the next red.
Preserve simple access to the remaining reds.
After the reds are gone, clear the colours in sequence.
routines.success_criteria: Log your best single attempt out of 51, then note how many full 3-red clearances you complete in 10 attempts.

altVideo.title: Snooker Practice | 3 Reds Break Building | Snooker Lesson

routines.name: Break Building Foundations
routines.summary: Build break-building habits through repeatable, low-risk scoring patterns.
routines.description: Focus on open reds, key-ball awareness, and controlled cue-ball movement in the scoring area.
routines.setup_instructions: Open 8-10 reds around the pink and black area.
steps: Choose a simple starter red.
Play for the highest-percentage colour each time.
Stop after each breakdown and review the shot or positional error that caused it.
routines.success_criteria: Log total points scored for the session. Also track the number of visits above 20 and how often the first red leads to a controlled scoring chance.

routines.name: Shots Around The Pink
routines.summary: Positional control routine built around pink-ball angles.
routines.description: Improve precision around the pink and nearby reds while keeping the cue-ball on the correct side of the shot.
routines.setup_instructions: Place two reds near the pink with different approach angles.
steps: Alternate between the two reds each visit.
Land on the preferred angle for the pink each time.
Complete 10 cycles without losing position on the pink.
routines.success_criteria: Log total points scored for the session while holding the correct angle on the pink; use cycle completion as your quality check.

video.title: Snooker Practice - Two Reds & Pink - Snooker Lesson

routines.name: Snooker Safety Shots off Reds
routines.summary: Touch-based safety drill off reds to leave the cue-ball safe in baulk.
routines.description: Practise thin safety contacts that send the cue-ball back to baulk while nudging the red towards the black end.
routines.setup_instructions: Use one red at a time in 6 positions along a line parallel to the top cushion, starting level with the black spot. Play each attempt with the cue-ball in hand from the D.
steps: From each position, contact the red with controlled pace and return the cue-ball towards the baulk cushion area.
Try to finish behind a baulk colour while moving the red back towards the black end.
Score each shot out of 3: cue-ball cover, distance into baulk, and whether the red finishes safe.
routines.success_criteria: Target 12+ points out of 18 per round. Log each round separately and watch the average.

routines.name: Escape Science Drill
routines.summary: Systematic escape training from common snookers.
routines.description: Build reliable escape percentages from the types of snookers players face most often in frames.
routines.setup_instructions: Create 10 snookers using the colours and baulk-line positions as the covering balls.
steps: Name the intended contact point before the shot.
Play a legal escape while still considering where the cue-ball will finish.
Record whether you made the hit and whether the resulting safety was acceptable.
routines.success_criteria: 2 points for legal escape + safe leave, 1 for legal hit only (max 20).

routines.name: Two Cushion Escape Drill
routines.summary: Improve reliability on two-cushion escape paths.
routines.description: Teaches contact references and pace for common two-cushion escapes.
routines.setup_instructions: Set 8 snookers where the direct path is blocked but a two-cushion escape is available.
steps: Pick the cushion contact point.
Play with positive, controlled pace.
Repeat each setup from both sides.
routines.success_criteria: Legal-hit percentage over 16 attempts (each snooker played from both sides).

video.title: Snooker escapes - Mastering 1, 2, 3 cushions escapes (Know How)

routines.name: Three Cushion Escape Drill
routines.summary: Advanced escape-path work for deep snookers.
routines.description: Practise three-cushion escapes for positions where safer one- or two-cushion paths are not available.
routines.setup_instructions: Set 6 difficult snookers where one- and two-cushion escapes are either blocked or very low percentage.
steps: Visualise the full three-cushion path before you play.
Control pace so you avoid leaving an easy chance.
Grade each attempt for both legality and the quality of the safety left behind.
routines.success_criteria: Track legal-hit percentage and safe-leave percentage separately.

routines.name: Straight Potting Reds
routines.summary: A straight-potting drill designed to identify weaknesses in cue alignment, delivery and aiming accuracy.
routines.description: Practise potting all 15 reds from a consistent position, using a straight line of balls across the table. The routine helps reveal whether you tend to miss shots to one side, allowing you to identify and correct repeated aiming or cueing errors.
routines.setup_instructions:
Arrange all 15 reds in a horizontal line across the table, running from the yellow side towards the green side. Space them evenly, approximately 4 inches apart, with the centre red positioned on the table's centre line.

Position the cue ball in baulk, directly in line with each red and its intended top corner pocket. The aim is to play each red as a straight pot.
steps: Work through all 15 reds, attempting to pot each one into its intended top corner pocket.
Use a centre-ball strike and focus on keeping your cue delivery straight.
Avoid changing your technique to compensate for each shot; aim to maintain the same consistent delivery.
Pay attention to which side of the pocket each missed red travels towards.
routines.success_criteria:
2 points – Red is potted cleanly.
1 point – Red rattles in the jaws but still drops.
0 points – Red is missed.

Record your total score after attempting all 15 reds.

routines.name: Long Blues
routines.summary: Improve your long-range potting accuracy and consistency by playing straight blue pots from distance.
routines.description:
This routine focuses on developing accuracy and confidence when playing long straight pots. Players must pot the blue into a corner pocket from progressively longer distances, concentrating on maintaining a straight cue action and consistent delivery.

By repeating the same type of shot across multiple attempts, players can identify weaknesses in their alignment, aiming and cue delivery.

The objective is to consistently pot the blue from distance while developing a reliable technique that can be transferred into match situations.
routines.setup_instructions:
This routine uses the blue ball positioned on its normal spot, with the cue ball placed directly in line with a corner pocket at the opposite end of the table. The distance between the cue ball and blue creates a challenging long straight pot.

Players should focus on maintaining a straight line of aim, delivering the cue smoothly and striking the centre of the cue ball. The setup should remain consistent throughout all 10 attempts so that players can accurately measure their potting performance.
steps: Place the blue ball on its normal spot.
Position the cue ball towards the opposite end of the table.
Align the cue ball, blue and chosen corner pocket in a straight line.
Ensure there is a significant distance between the cue ball and blue.
Check that the intended pocket is unobstructed.
Prepare to play a controlled, straight pot on the blue.
Repeat for 10 attempts, resetting the cue ball to the same position after each shot.
routines.success_criteria: Complete 10 attempts. Players receive 1 point for every successful pot.

routines.name: Free Up the Cueing Arm
routines.summary: Loose-arm warm-up session focused on flow and relaxed cue delivery.
routines.description: A lower-pressure reds-only session used to free the cueing arm and rebuild smooth rhythm.
routines.setup_instructions: Place 15 reds in a straight central line up the table and choose a starting red nearer the baulk end.
steps: Pot reds in order or in a chosen sequence while keeping the cue-ball off the cushions where possible.
Stay loose through the grip and cueing arm, prioritising rhythm over power.
Either reset after every miss for a stricter practice mode, or continue the visit for a confidence-building mode.
routines.success_criteria: Log total points scored out of 15 reds per set, then track cueing smoothness and visit quality across sets.

video.title: SNOOKER CUEING - The Secret To Good Snooker

routines.name: Cue Ball Control
routines.summary: Five-tip-position drill for understanding top, stun and screw response.
routines.description: Learn cue-ball behaviour by striking different heights on the vertical centre line of the cue-ball.
routines.setup_instructions: Place blue on blue spot. Place cue-ball about 10 inches (250mm) away on a straight line to the middle pocket. Use five tip heights: maximum top (about a tip above centre), half a tip above centre, dead centre, half a tip below centre, and maximum screw (about a tip below centre). Never strike beyond a tip from centre or you will miscue.
steps: Play 5 shots from each tip-height position with a smooth, standard cue action.
Observe whether the cue-ball runs through, holds, or screws back, and by how much.
Keep the arm and grip relaxed and deliver fully through the cue-ball.
routines.success_criteria: Log cue-ball finish outcomes for all 25 shots and note repeatability per tip height.

routines.name: Stun Run Through
routines.summary: Develop your ability to control the cue ball's forward movement after contact, using a stun run-through to achieve accurate positional play.
routines.description:
This routine focuses on developing a controlled stun run-through and improving your understanding of how cue action, tip placement and shot pace influence the cue ball's movement.

Players must pot the blue into the middle pocket while allowing the cue ball to continue forward towards a designated target area. By adjusting the amount of stun and the pace of the shot, players learn to control how far the cue ball travels after striking the object ball.

The objective is to consistently pot the blue and leave the cue ball as close as possible to the target, developing the touch and precision needed for effective positional play.
routines.setup_instructions:
This routine uses a straight blue pot into the middle pocket, with an additional object ball positioned beyond the blue to act as a positional target. The target ball provides a visual reference for where the cue ball should finish after completing the stun run-through.

The cue ball, blue and target ball should all be aligned towards the middle pocket. Players should aim to pot the blue and control the cue ball's forward movement, finishing as close to the target ball as possible without necessarily making contact with it
steps: Place the blue ball on its normal spot.
Position the cue ball directly in line with the blue and the middle pocket.
Place a second object ball beyond the blue, towards the middle pocket, along the same shot line.
Leave approximately one ball-width between the blue and the target ball.
Ensure the cue ball, blue and target ball are aligned in a straight line.
Check that the target ball is positioned in the path of the cue ball after the blue is potted.
1. Prepare to strike the cue ball around its centre, adjusting the pace to achieve a controlled run-through.
routines.success_criteria:
Complete 10 attempts. Players are scored on their ability to pot the blue and control the cue ball's final position relative to the target ball.

Blue potted and cue ball finishes within one ball-width of target = 2
Blue potted and cue ball finishes within two ball-widths of target = 1
Blue missed or cue ball finishes outside the target area  = 0

routines.name: Top Spin Control
routines.summary: Develop your ability to apply topspin and control the cue ball's forward movement, following the object ball into the pocket.
routines.description:
This routine focuses on developing a consistent topspin technique and understanding how striking the cue ball above its centre affects its movement after contact.

Players must pot the blue into the middle pocket while applying enough topspin to make the cue ball continue forward. The aim is to develop a smooth cue action, accurate tip placement and greater control over cue ball movement.
routines.setup_instructions: The routine uses a straightforward pot on the blue to isolate and practise the fundamentals of topspin. By positioning the cue ball directly in line with the blue and the middle pocket, players can focus entirely on their cue action and the amount of topspin applied.
steps: Place the blue ball on its normal spot.
Position the cue ball directly in line with the blue and the middle pocket.
Leave a comfortable distance between the cue ball and the blue.
Ensure the shot is straight towards the middle pocket.
Prepare to strike the cue ball just above its centre.
routines.success_criteria:
2 points for potting the blue and following through into the middle pocket, 1 point for potting the blue with forward cue ball movement, 0 points otherwise.
10 Attempts

routines.name: Side Spin Control
routines.summary: Learn how to apply left and right side spin to influence the cue ball's rebound off a cushion and improve positional control.
routines.description:
This routine focuses on understanding how side spin affects the cue ball when it contacts a cushion. Players will practise applying both left and right side spin, observing how the cue ball reacts differently depending on which side of the ball is struck.

By potting the blue and directing the cue ball towards a cushion, players can develop a better understanding of how side spin influences the rebound angle and subsequent cue ball position.

The objective is to consistently control the cue ball's path after contacting the cushion, developing the confidence to use side spin in match situations.
routines.setup_instructions:
This routine uses the blue ball and middle pocket to create a potting opportunity, with the cue ball travelling towards a side cushion after contact. A target ball is positioned in the area where the player should aim to bring the cue ball after its rebound.

Players will complete attempts using both left and right side spin, comparing how each changes the cue ball's path off the cushion. The target provides a reference for judging accuracy and developing a feel for how much side is required.
steps: Place the blue ball on its normal spot.
Position the cue ball at an angle that allows the blue to be potted into the middle pocket.
Ensure the cue ball's natural path after contact with the blue takes it towards a side cushion.
Place a target ball near the intended area of the cue ball's rebound.
Start by striking the cue ball to the left of centre to apply left side spin.
Pot the blue and observe the cue ball's rebound off the cushion.
Repeat the shot using right side spin.
Adjust the amount of side spin to bring the cue ball closer to the target.
routines.success_criteria:
Complete 10 attempts, alternating between left and right side spin.

Blue potted and cue ball finishes within one ball-width of target = 2
Blue potted and cue ball finishes within two ball-widths of target = 1
Blue missed or cue ball finishes outside the target area = 0

video.title: How To Aim With Side Correctly

altVideo.title: Snooker | Ultimate Guide to Side Spin | Tutorial

routines.name: Mastering Stun Shots
routines.summary: Master the stun shot by practising from different distances and learning how tip placement and cue pace influence the cue ball's behaviour after contact.
routines.description:
This routine focuses on developing a deeper understanding of stun shots and how they behave at different distances. Players will practise potting the blue into the middle pocket from progressively increasing distances, adjusting their cue action, tip placement and pace to achieve a consistent stun.

As the distance between the cue ball and object ball increases, players must understand how the cue ball's backspin naturally reduces during its journey across the table. This means adjustments to tip placement and cue delivery are required to achieve the desired stun at the point of contact.

The objective is to develop the ability to judge and execute stun shots from a variety of distances, giving players greater control over the cue ball and improving their positional play.
routines.setup_instructions:
This routine uses the blue ball on its normal spot, with the middle pocket as the target. The cue ball is positioned directly in line with the blue, but its starting distance changes throughout the exercise.

Players begin with a relatively short distance before gradually moving the cue ball further away. At each distance, they must adjust their technique to achieve a stun, where the cue ball stops or has minimal forward or backward movement after contacting the blue.
steps: Place the blue ball on its normal spot.
Identify a straight line between the blue and the middle pocket.
Position the cue ball approximately 6 inches from the blue.
Ensure the cue ball is directly aligned with the blue and middle pocket.
Begin by playing a stun shot, aiming to pot the blue while stopping the cue ball as close as possible to the point of contact.
Move the cue ball approximately 6 inches further away.
Repeat the shot, adjusting your tip placement and cue delivery to maintain the stun.
Continue increasing the distance until you are playing from approximately 3 feet away.
Repeat the exercise, focusing on maintaining consistency at each distance.
routines.success_criteria:
Complete 10 attempts across different distances. Players are scored on their ability to pot the blue and achieve the intended stun.

Blue potted and cue ball stops where the blue was = 2
Blue potted and cue ball has slight unwanted forward or backward movement = 1
Blue missed or cue ball travels significantly away from the intended position = 0

routines.name: Soft Screw Drill
routines.summary: Develop your ability to apply controlled backspin and bring the cue ball backwards a short distance after potting the object ball.
routines.description:
This routine focuses on developing a soft screw technique, teaching players how to generate enough backspin to bring the cue ball backwards without pulling it too far away from the object ball.

Players must pot the blue into the middle pocket while applying a controlled amount of backspin. The aim is to bring the cue ball back towards a designated target area, developing a better feel for tip placement, cue action and shot pace.

The objective is to achieve a consistent, gentle screw-back rather than relying on power, helping players improve their touch and positional accuracy.
routines.setup_instructions:
This routine uses a straight blue pot into the middle pocket, with an additional object ball positioned behind the blue to act as a reference for the cue ball's finishing position. The cue ball is placed in line with both balls, allowing players to practise a soft screw and judge how much backward movement they can generate.

The target ball provides a visual reference for the desired finishing position. Players should aim to pot the blue and bring the cue ball backwards towards the target, stopping as close as possible without necessarily making contact.
steps: Place the blue ball on its normal spot.
Position the cue ball directly in line with the blue and the middle pocket.
Place a second object ball behind the blue, towards the baulk end of the table.
Leave approximately one ball-width between the blue and the target ball.
Ensure all three balls are aligned towards the middle pocket.
Aim to strike the cue ball just below its centre.
Use a smooth, controlled cue action to generate a gentle screw-back.
Aim to pot the blue and bring the cue ball backwards towards the target.
routines.success_criteria:
Complete 10 attempts. Players are scored on their ability to pot the blue and bring the cue ball back towards the target.

Blue potted and cue ball finishes within one ball-width of target = 2
Blue potted and cue ball finishes within two ball-widths of target = 1
Blue missed or cue ball finishes outside the target area = 0

video.title: 3 Reasons Why You Can't Screw Back!

altVideo.title: Snooker Spin Screw Back Maximum Back Spin

routines.name: Deep Screw Drill
routines.summary: Develop your ability to generate powerful backspin and screw the cue ball backwards into the middle pocket after potting the blue
routines.description:
This routine focuses on developing a strong, controlled screw-back technique. Unlike the soft screw exercise, players must generate enough backspin to make the cue ball travel a greater distance backwards after striking the object ball.

Players must pot the blue into the middle pocket while applying deep screw, aiming to bring the cue ball all the way back into the same pocket. This helps develop confidence in striking low on the cue ball, maintaining a smooth cue action and generating consistent backspin.

The objective is to successfully pot both the blue and the cue ball into the middle pocket, developing the ability to generate substantial backspin while maintaining potting accuracy.
routines.setup_instructions:
This routine uses a straight blue pot into the middle pocket, with the cue ball positioned further away to allow enough distance for the cue ball to generate and maintain backspin. Unlike the soft screw routine, there is no additional target ball required, as the middle pocket itself becomes the finishing target.

Players must strike the cue ball well below its centre, using a smooth but committed cue action to generate enough backspin to bring it back towards the pocket after the blue has been potted.
steps: Place the blue ball on its normal spot.
Position the cue ball directly in line with the blue and the middle pocket.
Leave a suitable distance between the cue ball and the blue to allow for a deep screw shot.
Ensure the cue ball, blue and middle pocket are aligned in a straight line.
Aim to strike the cue ball below its centre to generate substantial backspin.
Use a smooth, accelerating cue action to maintain the backspin through contact.
Aim to pot the blue and screw the cue ball backwards into the same middle pocket.
routines.success_criteria:
Complete 10 attempts. Players are scored on their ability to pot the blue and bring the cue ball backwards into the middle pocket.

Blue potted and cue ball screws back into the middle pocket = 2
Blue potted and cue ball travels backwards but misses the pocket	= 1
Blue missed or cue ball fails to travel backwards	= 0

video.title: How To Play The Long Deep Screw Back | Snooker

routines.name: Long Reds – The Pink Opener
routines.summary: Improve your long-red potting accuracy while developing the cue ball control needed to hold position for the pink.
routines.description:
This routine focuses on combining long potting with controlled stun shots to develop a reliable opening shot in snooker. Players must pot a long red into a top corner pocket while controlling the cue ball's movement to leave themselves a comfortable opportunity on the pink.

The exercise encourages players to develop confidence when attempting difficult opening reds, while understanding the importance of cue ball control immediately after potting.

The objective is not simply to pot the red, but to consistently leave the cue ball in a suitable position for the pink, helping develop the skills required to turn opening opportunities into breaks.
routines.setup_instructions:
This routine uses the pink on its normal spot, with a red positioned approximately one foot away towards a top corner pocket. The cue ball is placed further back towards the baulk end, directly in line with the red and the intended pocket.

The distance creates a challenging long red, while the positioning encourages players to use a stun shot to hold the cue ball close to the red's original position. This should leave a natural opportunity to pot the pink after successfully potting the red.
steps: Place the pink ball on its normal spot.
Position a red approximately one foot away from the pink, towards a top corner pocket.
Align the red with the chosen top corner pocket.
Place the cue ball further back towards the baulk end, directly in line with the red and pocket.
Position the cue ball approximately halfway between the blue spot and the baulk colours.
Ensure the pink remains available as the intended next shot.
Prepare to play a long red using a controlled stun shot.
Repeat the exercise from the opposite side of the table to practise both left and right angles.
routines.success_criteria:
Complete 10 attempts from each side (20 attempts total).

2 points – Pot the long red and successfully stun the cue ball into the target area, leaving a good position for the pink and pot it.

1 point – Pot the red, but the cue ball doesn't finish in the target area.

0 points – Miss the red.

routines.name: Potting The Black Ball
routines.summary: Black-spot repetition drill for angle control and position discipline.
routines.description: Repeated black pots sharpen potting line, touch, and composure in the main scoring area.
routines.setup_instructions: Place the black on its spot. Start the cue-ball level with the black, about halfway to the side cushion, for a three-quarter-ball angle. Move it further towards the cushion for half-ball and then quarter-ball angles.
steps: Begin with straightforward blacks into the corner pockets and build towards tougher angles.
Keep the pattern simple and prioritise cue-ball control for the next black.
Track makes and the type of miss as the angle widens or the cue-ball drifts towards the cushions.
routines.success_criteria: Best uninterrupted black run and total makes per 25-ball set.

video.title: The best angle on the black!

altVideo.title: Why I Missed An Easy Pot.. Explained to try to stop it happening. (Snooker T Practice Routine)

routines.name: Reds and the Blue
routines.summary: Blue-ball break-building drill for when the pink and black are unavailable.
routines.description: Practise controlling the angle on the blue so you can keep bringing reds into play around the middle of the table.
routines.setup_instructions: Place all colours on their spots. Set 3 reds between the blue and brown spots and 3 between the blue and pink spots, spread along the centre line, 6 reds in total to start.
steps: Start with a red-to-blue pattern and aim to stay on the correct side of the blue.
Use fine pace so the cue-ball travels the minimum distance between shots.
When you clear 6 reds consistently, add extra reds to make the pattern tougher.
routines.success_criteria: Record total points scored per set; also track full-clear count and red-to-blue conversion as supporting quality metrics.

video.title: Snooker Blue Ball Common Shots PART 2 - Snooker Lesson

routines.name: Black Spot Builder: Level 1
routines.summary: Two reds either side of the black. Clear them using stun and screw, without the white touching a cushion.
routines.description: This is the first of three levels that build your breaks one step at a time. Everything happens around the black spot, so it’s all about short, controlled cue ball movement. Using stun and screw, you keep the white in a small area and always leave yourself the next pot. The best clearances never let the white touch a cushion. Once you can clear it within 5 attempts, move on to Level 2.
routines.setup_instructions: Black on its spot, with a red either side of it on the same line, a little under halfway to each side cushion. Put the white slightly to the right of the black and about 25 cm up the table, towards the pink.
steps: Pot a red into a corner pocket, using stun or screw to stop the white near the black.
Pot the black, controlling the white so you’re on the other red.
Pot the second red, then the black again.
Finish by potting the black as the last colour, for 23.
Keep the white within a short distance of the black spot. The challenge is never touching a cushion.
routines.success_criteria: Log your best attempt out of 5. Note how many attempts it took to clear the table, and move on to Level 2 when you clear it within 5.

routines.name: Black Spot Builder: Level 2
routines.summary: A third red joins, between the pink and the black. Getting position on it is the key shot.
routines.description: Level 2 adds one red, and that red changes how you play the black. Hard stun or screw won’t get you onto it. You need a soft stun that lets the white drift on past the red and stop in position. It teaches you to control how far the white travels, not just whether it stops. Once you can clear it within 5 attempts, move on to Level 3.
routines.setup_instructions:
Same as Level 1: black on its spot, a red either side of it, and the white slightly right of the black, about 25 cm up the table.
Plus a red just below the pink spot, on the line between the pink and the black.
steps: Start on either red beside the black.
For the red below the pink, pot the black with a soft stun and let the white drift past that red into position.
Take the black after each red where you can.
Finish by potting the black as the last colour.
If the white gets stuck behind a ball, reset and count it as an attempt.
routines.success_criteria: Log your best attempt out of 31. Note how many attempts it took to clear the table, and move on to Level 3 when you clear it within 5. An attempt ends when you miss or foul. 31 is three lots of red 1 + black 7 (24), then the last black 7.

routines.name: Black Spot Builder: Level 3
routines.summary: Five reds and all the colours. Split the reds early so your break keeps going.
routines.description: Level 3 is the closest to a real frame. Three of the reds are touching just below the pink, so you have to open them up to keep scoring. The skill is planning ahead: split the reds early with the black, and keep a red beside the black as a backup in case the split doesn’t leave you on a red. You don’t have to take the black every time. The aim is the biggest break you can make, and a total clearance is 67.
routines.setup_instructions:
All the colours on their spots.
Three touching reds just below the pink, between the pink and the black.
A red either side of the black, as in Level 1.
The white slightly right of the black, about 25 cm up the table.
steps: Open with a red beside the black, and use the black to split the three reds below the pink.
Keep the other red beside the black as a backup, in case you don’t land on one of the split reds.
Take whichever colour keeps the break going. It doesn’t have to be the black every time.
Once the reds are gone, clear the colours in order: yellow, green, brown, blue, pink, black.
Play for 20–30 minutes, resetting after each break.
routines.success_criteria: Log your highest break from the session, out of 67. Note how many full clearances you made. A break ends when you miss or foul. 67 is five lots of red 1 + black 7 (40), then the colours 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 (27).

routines.name: The Break Off
routines.summary: Develop your break-off technique by using left and right side spin to influence the cue ball's movement off the cushions and improve your safety positioning.
routines.description:
This routine focuses on introducing side spin into the snooker break-off, helping players understand how left and right side affect the cue ball's reaction when contacting cushions.

Players will practise breaking off from the D, sending the cue ball into the pack of reds and controlling its return towards the baulk end of the table. By experimenting with different amounts of side spin, players can observe how the cue ball reacts off the cushions and how this influences their final safety position.

The objective is to develop a consistent break-off while gaining a better understanding of side spin, cushion reactions and positional control.
routines.setup_instructions:
This routine uses a standard snooker break-off arrangement, with all 15 reds positioned in their usual triangle formation and the cue ball placed inside the D. Players will practise using both left and right side spin when playing the break-off, observing how the cue ball reacts after contacting the pack and cushions.

The aim is to achieve a controlled break-off, leaving the cue ball safely positioned towards the baulk end of the table. Players should complete attempts using both sides of the cue ball to compare the differences in rebound and positioning.
steps: Arrange all 15 reds in their standard triangle formation.
Ensure the pink and black are positioned on their usual spots.
Place the cue ball inside the D.
Line up a standard break-off shot towards the pack of reds.
Begin by striking slightly to the left of the cue ball's centre.
Play the break-off with controlled pace, aiming to contact the pack and return towards the baulk end.
Repeat the break-off using right side spin.
Observe how the cue ball reacts differently and adjust the amount of side to improve your safety position.
routines.success_criteria:
Complete 10 break-off attempts, alternating between left and right side spin.

Successful break-off with cue ball finishing safely in the baulk area = 2
Successful break-off but cue ball finishes outside the intended safety area= 	1
Foul, missed pack or poor break-off execution= 0

routines.name: Pink & Reds – Middle Pocket Practice
routines.summary: Develop your potting accuracy and break-building ability by clearing a line of reds and the pink into the middle pockets.
routines.description:
This routine focuses on developing consistency when potting reds and the pink into the middle pockets. With four or five reds arranged in a straight line between the pink and blue spots, players are presented with a structured sequence of shots.

Players must pot each red into either middle pocket before returning to the pink, developing their ability to control the cue ball and maintain position for the next shot.

The objective is to clear all the reds and the pink while maintaining a consistent rhythm, accurate potting and effective cue ball positioning.
routines.setup_instructions:
This routine uses the pink ball on its normal spot, with four or five reds arranged in a straight line between the pink and blue spots. The reds should be evenly spaced to create a consistent series of potting opportunities towards the middle pockets.

Players will work through the reds one at a time, alternating between potting a red and returning to the pink. This creates a repetitive break-building exercise that encourages players to develop consistent cue ball positioning and accurate middle-pocket potting.
steps: Place the pink ball on its normal spot.
Place four or five reds in a straight line between the pink and blue spots.
Space the reds evenly along the line.
Ensure the reds are positioned centrally along the line between the two spots.
Leave both middle pockets available as potting targets.
Begin by potting the first red into either middle pocket.
Follow the red by potting the pink into a middle pocket.
Continue alternating between the remaining reds and the pink until all reds have been cleared.
routines.success_criteria:
Players complete the routine for 15 minutes, attempting to pot as many reds and pinks as possible while following the correct sequence.

The player records their highest break achieved during the session. If they miss a pot or break the sequence, their break ends and they start again.

routines.name: Colours Clearance – Starting from Blue
routines.summary: Practise clearing all six colours in sequence, starting with the blue and finishing on the black.
routines.description: A colour-clearance routine designed to improve positional play, shot selection and potting consistency. Start by potting the blue, then work through the remaining colours in their normal order, aiming to leave position on each next colour.
routines.setup_instructions: Place all six colours on their usual spots: yellow, green, brown, blue, pink and black. The cue ball starts in a suitable position to pot the blue.
steps: Place all six colours on their normal spots.
Position the cue ball for a pot on the blue.
Ensure the colours are respotted after each pot, as they would be during a normal clearance.
The clearance begins with the blue and follows the standard colour order.
routines.success_criteria:
The player repeats the routine, resetting the colours each time, and tries to complete as many full clearances as possible within the 15-minute session.

1 count – Complete the entire clearance from blue through to black without missing.

0 counts – Fail to complete the clearance.

routines.name: Mercedes
routines.summary: A structured red-and-pink practice routine designed to improve break building and positional play.
routines.description: Practise building a break from the traditional Mercedes red formation. The reds are arranged in a Y shape around the pink, creating different angles and positional challenges. The aim is to pot the reds and pinks in sequence while maintaining control of the cue ball.
routines.setup_instructions: Place the pink on its normal spot and arrange all 15 reds in a Y formation around it.
steps: Place the pink on its normal spot.
Arrange 5 reds in a straight line above the pink, towards the top cushion.
Arrange 5 reds diagonally down the left side of the pink.
Arrange the remaining 5 reds diagonally down the right side.
Leave enough space between the reds to allow individual pots and cue-ball movement.
routines.success_criteria: Record your highest break achieved during the session. Use normal snooker scoring:
